formulas.formula: A simple, step-by-step budget for beginners. Works with any pay schedule.
Your goals add up to (aim for 100%):
1. In YOUR SETUP above, type your budget year (optional). It shows on every month and the dashboard.
2. Your 50 / 30 / 20 goals are in YOUR SETUP too. Change them once and every month follows.
3. Go to the month you're starting (for example Jan). Under PAYCHECKS & INCOME, add each paycheck you get.
4. In MONTHLY SPENDING, type a Planned amount for each category before the month starts.
5. As you spend, type the real amounts in the Actual column. Difference shows if you're over or under.
6. Check THE 50 / 30 / 20 CHECK near the bottom of each month to see how balanced your spending is.
7. Use Bills to tick off bills as you pay them, Savings Goals for your goals and Debt Payoff for debts.
8. Open the Dashboard anytime to see your whole year at a glance.
9. Need more lines? On a month tab, use the 'Other' rows or insert a row inside a list. On Bills, Savings Goals and Debt Payoff, use the blank rows.
10. January has example numbers so you can see how it works. Delete them and type your own.
Your year at a glance: totals, savings rate, charts, goals and debt.
One tab per month: paychecks, planned vs. actual spending, the 50/30/20 check and a chart.
Every month side by side, with yearly totals, monthly averages and a chart.
A checklist of your monthly bills. Tick a box when a bill is paid.
Track goals with progress bars and see how many months you have to go.
See how long each debt will take and which to pay first (snowball order).
A beginner's guide: the 50/30/20 rule, emergency funds, debt tips and more.
White cells: type your numbers here.
Tinted cells: these calculate for you. No typing needed.
Red: over budget, or something to fix (like text typed into a number cell).
Green: on track or under budget.
Thank you for your purchase! Happy budgeting.

Tip: start with an Emergency Fund of $1,000, then build it up to 3-6 months of your needs.
Snowball: pay the minimum on everything, and put every extra dollar on the SMALLEST balance first (Snowball Order 1). Quick wins keep you motivated.
Avalanche: put extra money on the HIGHEST interest rate first. You pay less interest overall.
When one debt is paid off, add its payment to the next one. That's how the snowball grows.
Months to Pay Off is for each debt on its own at its Total Payment. Rolling paid-off payments into the next debt gets you debt-free sooner than LONGEST shows.
Type the APR as 22.99% or just 22.99. 'Payment too low' means the payment doesn't cover the monthly interest yet.

formulas.formula: A budget is a plan for your money. Before the month starts, you decide where each dollar will go.
Then you track what really happens and adjust. That's it: plan, track, adjust.
You don't need to be perfect. Every month you budget, you get better at it.
A simple starting point for splitting your take-home pay (the money that actually hits your account).
Your goals are in YOUR SETUP on the Start Here tab (50 / 30 / 20 to start). Based on your average income:
Needs: rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, minimum debt payments
Wants: dining out, shopping, subscriptions, fun
Savings & debt payoff: emergency fund, goals, extra debt payments
Your average monthly income so far (from the Year Overview):
="If your needs are more than "&TEXT(Dashboard!$L$29,"0%")&", that's okay. Start where you are and adjust a little each month."
On each monthly tab, plan your spending until 'Not planned yet' reaches $0.
Money without a plan tends to disappear. Even $20 gets a job, like 'Savings' or 'Fun Money'.
Step 1: save a starter fund of $1,000 for surprises like car repairs or a doctor visit.
Step 2: grow it to 3 months of your needs. For you that's about:
Step 3 (the gold standard): 6 months of your needs:
Keep it in a separate savings account so you aren't tempted to spend it.
Snowball: smallest balance first for quick wins. Avalanche: highest interest rate first to save money.
Both work. The best method is the one you'll stick with. See the Debt Payoff tab.
1. Budget with your take-home pay, not your salary before taxes.
2. Pay yourself first: move savings out on payday, before you spend.
3. Plan for irregular costs (car repairs, gifts, yearly fees) with a small amount every month.
4. Check your bank account once a week. Five minutes is enough.
5. Use cash or a separate card for fun money so you can see when it runs out.
6. Wait 24 hours before any unplanned purchase over $50.
7. Cancel subscriptions you haven't used in a month.
8. Cook at home a few more nights a week; groceries cost less than takeout.
9. Celebrate small wins, like a paid-off card or your first $500 saved.
10. Over budget this month? No guilt. Adjust next month's plan and keep going.
Take-home pay (net pay): what you receive after taxes and deductions.
Fixed expense: the same every month, like rent. Variable expense: changes, like groceries.
Sinking fund: saving a little each month for a known future cost, like holidays.
APR: the yearly interest rate on a debt. Higher APR means more interest.
Emergency fund: money set aside only for real emergencies.
